subject: Cognitive Science
title: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Motivation
description: A short lesson to help you apply Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Motivation.

hook.text: Pay kids to read and they read more—until you stop paying. Then they read less than before.

buildup.text: Extrinsic motivation (rewards, grades) can crowd out intrinsic motivation (genuine curiosity).

discovery.text: Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory identifies three needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness.

twist.text: Not all rewards kill motivation. Unexpected praise and informational feedback actually boost it.

climax.text: The key is whether the reward controls behavior or acknowledges competence. Intent shapes impact.

punchline.text: Rewards can fuel or kill the desire to learn.

quiz.question: What does self-determination theory identify as core human needs?

details.summary: Intrinsic motivation comes from internal interest and enjoyment. Extrinsic motivation comes from external rewards or punishments. Research shows that adding extrinsic rewards to intrinsically motivated activities can actually undermine the original motivation, a phenomenon called the overjustificat.
details.whyItMatters: Misapplied rewards can destroy the love of learning. Understanding the interaction between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation is essential for education, parenting, and management.
takeaways: Intrinsic motivation is driven by internal interest
Extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation
The overjustification effect turns play into work

faq.question: What is the overjustification effect?
faq.answer: When children who enjoyed drawing were given awards for drawing, they drew less in free time afterwards. The external reward shifted their attribution from I draw because I enjoy it to I draw for rewards. Removing the reward removed the reason to draw.

faq.question: Are extrinsic rewards always harmful?
faq.answer: No. Extrinsic rewards work well for tasks that are not intrinsically interesting. They become problematic mainly when applied to activities people already enjoy.
